Activated folate (Quatrefolic®)
Supports energy production

Activated B2, B6 & B12
Activated folate (Quatrefolic®)
Supports energy production

cautions.text:
B vitamins are stimulatory in nature. To avoid any sleep interferance, avoid taking before bed.
Taking at night may result in more vivid dreams (vitamin B6).

interactions.interaction_text: Caution with cholestyramine and colestipol (hypolipidaemic agents)

may decrease the absorption of vitamin B3 and folate. Separate dose by at least 4-6 hours.
Caution with phenobarbital and phenytoin (anticonvulsants) - high doses of vitamin B6 or folate can decrease their efficacy. Monitor.
Caution with L-Dopa - vitamin B6 increases the peripheral metabolism of levodopa and may lower levodopa levels for CNS penetration, resulting in reduced levodopa effects. The effect of pyridoxine is prevented by administration of a dopa-decarboxylase inhibitor (e.g. benserazide, carbidopa) with levodopa, as is common clinical practice.
Caution with antiepileptic and anticonvulsant medications – folic acid may reduce serum levels of these medications. Patients should take folate only under the supervision of a health professional.
Caution with methotrexate (folic acid antagonist) - co-administrate with folate may reduce the effects. Patients should take folate only under the supervision of a health professional.
Caution with tetracycline hydrochloride (antibiotic) - B vitamins may reduce drug bioavailability. Separate dose by at least 2 hours.
Several medications may deplete folate status, including trimethoprim (antibiotic), pyrimethamine (antimalarial), triamterene (blood pressure), sulfasalazine (for ulcerative colitis) and oral contraceptives.
Several medications can decrease the absorption of vitamin B12 or increase the risk of deficiency, such as acid-suppressing medications (proton-pump inhibitors e.g. omeprazole and
histamine2 (h2)-receptor antagonists), metformin (hypoglycaemic), oral contraceptives, neomycin (antibiotic) and colchicine (anti-gout).

indications.text:
Biotin, also known as vitamin B7, forms part of the B vitamin family. Biotin is involved in cell growth, fatty acid production and in the metabolism of carbohydrates, fats and proteins.
Biotin is a water-soluble vitamin and is an essential cofactor for 5 carboxylase enzymes including:
Acetyl-coenzyme A (CoA) carboxylase 1 and acetyl-CoA carboxylase 2: binds bicarbonate to acetyl-CoA to form malonyl-CoA, required for the production of fatty acids.
Pyruvate carboxylase: critical for gluconeogenesis (formation of glucose from sources other than carbohydrates such as amino acids and fats).
Methylcrotonyl-CoQ carboxylase: essential step in the metabolism of the amino acid leucine.
Propionyl-CoA carboxylase: catalyses essential steps in the metabolism of amino acids, cholesterol and odd chain fatty acids.
Many foods contain small amounts of biotin and this depends greatly on the season. Foods that contain the most biotin include organ meats, eggs, fish, meat, seeds, nuts and certain vegetables including sweet potato.
Gastrointestinal enzymes break down the protein-bound forms of ingested biotin, which then undergo further processing by the
enzyme biotinidase in the intestinal lumen to release free biotin. The free biotin is then absorbed in the small intestine and most biotin is stored in the liver and central nervous system.
A diet high in raw egg whites can lead to a biotin deficiency. Raw egg whites are high in avidin, a protein that binds to biotin and inhibits its absorption. Cooking denatures avidin, making it unable to interfere with biotin absorption.
Signs and symptoms of biotin deficiency include skin rashes, brittle nails, thinning hair or hair loss.
Pregnancy increases biotin requirements as the fetus requires biotin for carboxylase reactions and DNA replication.
Hair, skin & nails
Biotin 3mg supports hair, skin and nail health. It plays a role in the normal structure and function of skin and mucous membranes. Biotin is a coenzyme for carboxylase enzymes that are involved in fatty acid synthesis, branched-chain amino acid catabolism and
gluconeogenesis, important for maintenance of healthy skin and hair.
Keratin is an important structural protein found in the epidermis. It is the key component of the hair, skin and nails. Keratin mainly functions to adhere cells to each other and to form a protective layer on the outside of the skin. Biotin plays a role in protein synthesis, specifically keratin production.
Biotin 3mg supports nail health, strength and thickness. Brittle nails are characterised by roughness of the surface of the nail plate, fragility and peeling. It is associated with an abnormality of keratin,
keratin associated proteins, water, and/or lipid content. Biotin appears to improve brittle nails by inducing epidermal differentiation.
In one study, 71 subjects with brittle fingernails were given 2.5mg of biotin per day. Out of the 45 subjects that completed the study, 91% showed a definite improvement with firmer and harder fingernails after an average treatment of 5.5±2.3 months1.
Another study investigated the effects of 2.5mg/day of biotin on brittle and splitting fingernails. A total of 32 subjects were placed into 3 groups: group A was the control (n=10), group B comprised subjects with brittle nails (n=8) studied before and after biotin supplementation, and group C included subjects with brittle nails in whom the administration of biotin did not coincide exactly with the initial and terminal clipping of the nails (n=14). The thickness of the nails in group B increased significantly by 25% and group C by 7%. Splitting of the nails were reduced in groups B and C and the irregular cellular arrangement of the dorsal surface of brittle nails became more regular in all nails of group B and in 8 of 11 nails of group C. Results were seen after 6 to 15 months of biotin supplementation2.

cautions.text: Biotin shares the sodium-dependent multivitamin transporter (SMVT) with vitamin B5. Theoretically, this may reduce vitamin B5 absorption due to competitive inhibition of the transporter.

indications.text:
Breastfeeding Support contains two herbs, Fenugreek and Blessed thistle, to support milk supply in breastfeeding women.
Fenugreek and Blessed thistle are herbal galactagogues. A galactagogue is a substance that promotes the secretion and flow of milk.
A 2015 qualitative study found that Fenugreek and Blessed thistle were the two most commonly used herbal galactagogues1.
Breastfeeding
During pregnancy, breasts change and develop to be ready to supply milk. The amount of breastmilk usually increases a few days after the birth, when the milk “comes in”.
The first milk produced after the birth is called colostrum, which is more concentrated than mature milk and rich in protein and antibodies. It is gradually replaced by mature milk.
When a baby sucks at the breast, it stimulates nerves in the nipple that release hormones into the blood stream. Prolactin activates milk-making tissues, while oxytocin causes the breast to let down the milk (“let-down reflex”).
Breastmilk is the normal food for babies, containing all the baby’s nutritional needs for the first 6 months of life, satisfying both hunger and thirst, and supporting the baby’s immune system. The act of breastfeeding also helps the baby’s jaw development. Breastfeeding benefits the mother by helping the uterus return to its normal size after childbirth.
One of the most common reasons mothers cease breastfeeding earlier than planned is because they feel they don’t have enough milk for their babies.
Fenugreek
Fenugreek is a herb native to the Mediterranean region, southern Europe and western Asia. It is traditionally used in Western herbal medicine as a nutritive tonic and galactagogue to increase breastmilk production in breastfeeding women.
The mechanism of action of Fenugreek on breastmilk is not fully understood, but it is suggested that Fenugreek stimulates sweat production, which then enhances milk secretion because the breast is a type of sweat gland. Fenugreek may also have oestrogenic activity.
A randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled study involving 66 mother-infant pairs assessed the effect of Fenugreek tea on breastmilk production. The mean measured breastmilk volume of
the mothers who received galactagogue tea was significantly higher than the placebo and control groups (p<0.05)2.
An anecdotal report of 1200 women taking 580mg or 610mg of Fenugreek three times a day stated that most women experienced an increase in milk supply within 24 to 72 hours of use3.
Fenugreek also supports healthy appetite.
Blessed thistle
Blessed thistle supports breastmilk production in breastfeeding women. It is believed to work by stimulating the flow of blood to the mammary glands, thereby enriching milk flow.
Blessed thistle is a weed native to the Mediterranean that has been used for over 2000 years to stimulate appetite, aid digestion and as a galactagogue. According to Grieves, “it is chiefly used now for nursing mothers the warm infusion scarcely ever failing to procure a proper supply of milk. It is considered one of the best medicines which can
be used for the purpose”4.

cautions.text: Contraindicated in pregnancy - Fenugreek can cause uterine contractions, increasing the risk of early labour or miscarriage.

interactions.interaction_text:
Caution with warfarin and other anticoagulant or antiplatelet drugs - Fenugreek may affect blood coagulation (based on an isolated case report). Monitor.
Caution with hypoglycaemic drugs - Fenugreek may have additive effects. Monitor blood glucose.
Caution with iron - Fenugreek can inhibit iron absorption. Separate dose by 2 hours.

Caution with aluminium salts (e.g. antacids) – calcium citrate may increase the absorption of aluminum. Separate dose.
Caution with bisphosphonates – calcium reduces drug absorption and may reduce effectiveness. Take bisphosphonates at least 30 minutes before calcium supplements.

indications.text:
Pau d’arco, also known as Red Lapacho or Taheebo, is a canopy tree native to the Amazon rainforest and can be found in tropical regions of South and Central America. Pau d’arco has been used by native Americans of Brazil, northern Argentina, Paraguay and Peru for over
1000 years, with a long history of medicinal use that pre-dates the Incas.
The bark of the Pau d’arco tree is hard and durable and well-known for its resistance to insect and fungal attack.
Pau d’arco is traditionally used in South American medicine to relieve symptoms of mild, superficial fungal skin infections. Traditionally, the bark/heartwood of Pau d’arco was prepared as a decoction or herbal tea and was prescribed for many ailments including fevers, sore throats, dysentery and snakebites as well as used topically for wounds and skin conditions.
Pau d’arco is also traditionally used in South American medicine to support gastrointestinal system health.
The inner stem bark of Pau d’arco naturally contains bioactive compounds called naphthoquinones and furanonapthoquinones that contribute significantly to the therapeutic activity of the herb.
Two main bioactive components have been isolated from Pau d’arco: lapachol and β-lapachone. These are key constituents responsible for the antifungal and antibacterial activity of Pau d’arco. The majority
of research has focused on the lapachol component, however, other napthoquinones and their furano derivatives are likely to contribute to the therapeutic activity of Pau d’arco.
Candida Relief contains Pau d’arco sourced from Brazil that has been HPLC tested for lapachol content to identify the plant species. Pau d’arco is commonly found to contain adulterants, so proper herbal identification and quality testing is essential.
Candida
Candida albicans (Candida) is a yeast-like fungus that normally inhabits the human microbiome, is present in small amounts on the skin and can be found in the mouth, digestive and reproductive tract.
Candida is a harmless, commensal yeast that exists in harmony with other yeasts and bacteria and is only considered a fungal pathogen when there is an overgrowth in certain areas of the body.
Candida overgrowth can lead to a condition called candidiasis. There are several types of candidiasis, the most common being:
Oral/oropharyngeal/oesophageal thrush: yeast infection in the mouth, throat and oesophageal area. Symptoms include white spots inside the mouth and on the tongue, redness, soreness and difficulty swallowing.
Genital thrush: most commonly experienced by women and characterised by extreme itching, soreness and redness in the vaginal area, accompanied by white clumpy vaginal discharge.
In men, the symptoms include a red rash on the penis and itching and burning on the tip of the penis.
A number of factors can lead to candida overgrowth including disruption to the pH of the environment, antibiotic use, a weakened immune system and immunosuppressants.
Antifungal activity
Pau d’arco supports healthy immune system function and relieves the symptoms of candida. Pau d’arco and its constituents lapachol and β-lapachone have demonstrated in vitro activity against various Candida species including Candida albicans and Candida tropicalis1. Bark extracts of Pau d’arco have also shown broad-spectrum activity in vitro, specifically active against most fungal strains2.
The mechanism of action may involve interference with the fungal cell membrane3. Napthoquinones are inhibitors of the electron transport chain and act by uncoupling oxidative phosphorylation, thus inhibiting ATP synthesis.
Several constituents found in Pau d’arco have also demonstrated antibacterial activity in vitro, including lapachol, β-lapachone and anthraquinone-2-carboxylic acid. These isolated compounds have shown activity against Helicobacter pylori, Clostridium perfringens, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Streptococcus faecalis, Enterococcus and Bacillus species, and various strains of Staphylococcus aureus4,5.
β-lapachone and other napthoquinone compounds have shown activity against methicillin-resistant staphylococcus aureus (MRSA), offering a potential synergistic effect with antimicrobial drugs6.

interactions.interaction_text:
Caution with hypoglycaemic medication - chromium may have an additive effect. Monitor blood sugar levels.
Caution with thyroxine – chromium can reduce drug absorption. Seperate dose by at least 3 hours.
Food sources rich in chromium include organ meats, cheese, broccoli,
green beans, spices and wine.
The absorption of chromium from the intestinal tract is low and can be enhanced by the intake of nutrients such as vitamin C and niacin. Chromium is stored in the liver, spleen, soft tissue and bone.
Diets high in simple sugars result in increased urinary chromium excretion in adults. This effect may be related to increased insulin secretion in response to the consumption of simple sugars compared to complex carbohydrates.
Stressors, such as elevated blood sugar, strenuous physical activity or work, infection and emotional and physical trauma, may increase the excretion of chromium.
Glucose metabolism
Chromium was first identified as ‘Glucose Tolerance Factor’, however, it was later discovered to be a complex of molecules found in the body comprised of chromium bound to single molecules of glycine, cysteine, glutamic acid, and two molecules of nicotinic acid.
Chromium MAX aids the metabolism of glucose and supports the cellular uptake of glucose. Low chromium levels are associated with impaired glucose, insulin and lipid metabolism.
Chromium can improve insulin sensitivity, aiding the ability of insulin to transport glucose into cells. Chromium seems to be transported to insulin-sensitive cells by transferrin in response to increases in
plasma insulin levels. It is suspected to potentiate insulin by increasing receptor numbers and affinity as well as increasing insulin binding to cells.
Food satiety
Chromium picolinate has been suggested to impact neurotransmitters involved in the regulation of eating behaviour, mood and food cravings.
An 8-week randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled study was performed to investigate the effects of chromium on food intake, satiety and cravings. A total of 42 healthy, overweight women who reported carbohydrate cravings were randomly assigned either 1000 micrograms/day of chromium picolinate or placebo. The group receiving chromium reported decreased food intake and hunger ratings by week 8. A decrease in cravings for carbohydrates, fast foods, high-fat foods and sweet was noted over time1.

interactions.interaction_text:
Caution with hypoglycaemic medications and insulin – GlucoPlex may have additive effects. Monitor.
Caution with warfarin – ALA has reduced platelet reactivity in vitro, uncertain whether the effect is clinically significant.
Caution with anticoagulant/antiplatelet drugs – Fenugreek may have additive effects, increasing the risk of bruising and bleeding.
Caution with thyroxine – ALA may suppress the conversion of thyroxine to active T3 form and chromium can reduce thyroxine absorption. Separate dose by 3 hours.
Caution with calcium channel blockers – vitamin D may reduce the effectiveness of these drugs.
Caution with digoxin – vitamin D can elevate serum calcium levels, which increases the risk of cardiac arrhythmias with digoxin. Monitor calcium levels.
Caution with thiazide diuretics – when taken in conjunction with vitamin D, can increase the risk of hypercalcaemia. Monitor serum calcium levels during concurrent use.
Caution with cholestyramine or colestipol (lipid-lowering medication) and orlistat – these drugs may reduce the absorption of fat-soluble vitamins, including vitamin D. Take one hour before, or 4-6 hours after drug.
Caution with NSAIDs, cefalexin, penicillamine and tetracycline and quinolone antibiotics - zinc forms complexes with these drugs, interfering with absorption. Separate dose by 3 hours.
Caution with iron supplements – Fenugreek and zinc can interfere with iron absorption. Separate dose by 2 hours.
Caution with copper and manganese supplementation – ALA can bind to minerals. Separate dose by 3 hours.

interactions.interaction_text:

Clinical significance is unclear. Caution is warranted with drugs with a narrow therapeutic range (e.g. barbiturates, digoxin, lithium, phenytoin, warfarin). Separate dose by 2 hours.

Caution with glucose lowering medications (including metformin) – Aloe vera given in conjunction with glucose-lowering medication may have additive effects. Potentially beneficial interaction.
Caution with thiazide diuretics, cardiac glycosides, corticosteroids (e.g. prednisolone) and stimulant laxatives - Licorice may potentiate hypokalaemia. However, the DGL form is considered safer and less likely to result in drug interactions.

Caution with NSAIDs, cefalexin, penicillamine and tetracycline and quinolone antibiotics – zinc forms chelates with the drugs, reducing absorption. Separate the dose by 3 hours.

indications.text:
Niacin is a water-soluble vitamin required for the function of over 200 enzymes throughout the body. It is well-absorbed after oral administration and metabolised in the liver to nicotinamide
adenine dinucleotide (NAD) and nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate (NADP). NAD and NADP are essential for energy metabolism, oxidation-reduction reactions and ADP-ribose transfer reactions involved in DNA repair and calcium mobilisation.
Niacin can be formed in the body from the amino acid tryptophan. It takes 60mg of tryptophan to make 1mg niacin. Poor protein intake, especially inadequate tryptophan, increases the risk of deficiency.
Niacin helps convert food into energy and assists in the metabolism of carbohydrates and dietary fats. It is a component of the glucose tolerance factor (GTF) that supports sugar metabolism.
Niacin supports skin health. It can dilate small blood vessels, improving blood flow of nutrients and oxygen to the skin, heart and brain.
Niacin is often used in high doses to maintain cardiovascular health and a healthy lipid profile. Niacin can reduce fibrinogen
concentrations in plasma and may stimulate fibrinolysis. It inhibits the mobilisation of free fatty acids from peripheral tissues and reduces hepatic synthesis of triglycerides and the secretion of low density lipoproteins and very low-density lipoproteins1.
Niacin vs nicotinamide
Two main forms of vitamin B3 are found in foods: nicotinic acid (niacin) and nicotinamide (niacinamide). Both can be converted into active forms of vitamin B3 in the body.
Both niacin and nicotinamide can perform all the essential biochemical functions of vitamin B3 in the body and prevent a deficiency, however, niacin has additional actions, such as cardiovascular effects and blood vessel dilation.
Nicotinamide does not cause the flush that is a common side effect of niacin supplementation.
Niacin flush
Niacin supplementation is commonly associated with flushing of the skin, known as the ‘niacin flush’, caused by the dilation of the capillaries. Although this effect is transient and harmless, it can be uncomfortable and concerning if people do not expect it.
The body usually adapts to niacin intake overtime and side-effects lessen in severity. Skin flushing is worse when niacin is taken on an empty stomach.
Flushing is usually caused by higher doses and immediate release niacin. Niacin 100mg Extended Release is unlikely to cause flushing.
Extended release
Niacin 100mg Extended Release is an extended-release product that releases niacin into the body over an 8-hour period. Extended-release forms are less likely to cause flushing than immediate-release forms.
It is important to differentiate extended-release from sustained-release forms. Sustained-release niacin preparations release niacin into the body over a 24-hour period and are associated with a higher risk of hepatotoxicity and gastrointestinal intolerance than unmodified niacin preparations. This may be because the liver is not given a break.
Extended-release niacin allows the vitamin to be absorbed over 8 hours, which reduces the incidence of flushing seen with immediate-release forms, and hepatotoxicity, seen with sustained-release forms, as it still allows the liver to have a break. Increased risk of hepatotoxicity is not seen with extended-release niacin2.

cautions.text:
Not recommended during pregnancy or lactation due to insufficient safety data on high doses of niacin.
Avoid consuming with alcohol. Alcohol can exacerbate the flushing associated with niacin.
Contraindicated in people with gout. Niacin can reduce urinary excretion of uric acid, potentially resulting in hyperuricemia.
Caution in people with blood sugar imbalance. High doses of niacin can impair glucose tolerance. However, doses under 1.5g daily have minimal effects on blood glucose.

interactions.interaction_text:
Caution with anticoagulant or antiplatelet medication - niacin may increase the risk of bleeding in some patients.
Caution with bile acid sequestrants (e.g. cholestyramine) – drugs bind to niacin and decrease absorption. Separate dose by 4-6 hours.
Caution with statin medication. Co-administration of statins and niacin may increase the risk of developing myotoxicity,
however, usually in much higher doses. Co-administration is often recommended for dyslipidaemia; it is recommended to use the lowest possible dose of both agents and monitor patient for signs of myotoxicity during concurrent use.

Caution with aspirin and paracetamol – zinc and vitamin A may reduce their effectiveness. Separate dose by 2 hours.
Caution with calcium supplements – zinc and calcium compete for common intestinal absorption sites. Separate supplements by at least 2 hours.
Caution with chemotherapeutic agents – evidence regarding the use of vitamin C in conjunction with chemotherapy treatment is still emerging. Use only under medical supervision.
Caution with aluminium based antacids – vitamin C increases the amount of aluminium absorbed. Separate dose by 2 hours.

cautions.text:
Contraindicated during pregnancy and lactation.
Discontinue use at least one week prior to any general anaesthetic.
Avoid St John’s wort in combination with tyramine-rich foods and beverages – coadministration may cause elevated blood pressure and rapid heart rate. Tyramine-rich foods include aged cheeses, cured meats, fermented foods, dried fruits, beer and red wine.

interactions.interaction_text:
St John’s wort, particularly hyperforin, induces the CYP450 enzyme system, and should not be used with drugs metabolised through this pathway, including indianvir, cyclosporin, oral contraceptives, digoxin, theophylline, HIV protease inhibitors, HIV non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors, methadone, antineoplastic drugs, anticonvulsants (phenobarbiton, phenytoin), antidepressants, tacrolimus, omeprazole, midazolam, alprazolam and carbamazepine (tegretol).
Contraindicated with anticoagulants warfarin (coumadin, marevan) and phenprocoumon - St John’s wort may decrease pro-thrombin time and international normalised ratio (INR) values. Monitor.
Contraindicated with oral contraceptives. St John’s wort may decrease efficacy and increase risk of ovulation and pregnancy.

indications.text:
Vitamin B1 (thiamine) is a water-soluble vitamin that is involved in carbohydrate metabolism and nervous system health. As body
reserves of thiamine are small, a steady intake is important to avoid deficiency. Vitamin B1 100mg helps prevent vitamin B1 deficiency.
There is approximately 30mg of thiamine in the average adult, with about half of this stored in muscle tissue. It is also found in high concentrations in the heart, liver, kidneys and brain1.
Vitamin B1 is absorbed in the small intestine. It is generally well absorbed, however, several dietary factors can decrease absorption, including alcohol, thiaminase, sulfite preservatives, high intakes of tea and coffee and folate or protein deficiency. A high alcohol intake is the greatest risk factor for thiamine deficiency, as alcohol both impairs the absorption and enhances the excretion of the vitamin, doubling the risk of deficiency.
Strenuous exercise, fever, excessive alcohol consumption, pregnancy and lactation and adolescent growth periods can increase thiamine requirements. The elderly may also have an increased requirement for thiamine.
Food sources of thiamine include meats, wheatgerm, wholegrain cereals, peas, beans and peanuts, milk, Brewer’s yeast and yeast extracts. Wheatgerm provides an important source of thiamine in the diet, however, thiamine is sensitive to heat and light, so can be lost in processing.
Thiamine hydrochloride is the most common form of supplemental vitamin B1. It consists of 89% thiamine and 11% hydrochloric acid.
Excess thiamine is cleared from the body via the kidneys; as such, there is no evidence of toxic effects from oral administration.
Energy
Vitamin B1 is converted to its active form in the body, thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP). TPP is a vital coenzyme in the production of energy within cells.
Vitamin B1 is required for normal digestion and the conversion of food into energy. It is a cofactor for several enzymes involved in carbohydrate catabolism, including pyruvate dehydrogenase,
transketolase and alpha-ketoglutarate. It is also involved in amino acid catabolism.
Due to its role in energy production, most of the body’s thiamine is stored in muscle.
A study found that supplementation with 10mg thiamine daily in women with a marginal deficiency lead to significantly increased general well-being and decreased fatigue2.
Nervous system
Vitamin B1 is important to maintain a healthy nervous system. It is located in the nerve cell membrane and is important for the transmission of nerve impulses.
Vitamin B1 plays a role in the metabolism of several neurotransmitters, including acetylcholine, GABA and serotonin, and, therefore, plays a role in maintaining healthy mood.
Hormones
A randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover study found that 100mg of vitamin B1 daily helped the symptoms of dysmenorrhoea and supplementation had lasting effects up to 3 months after the supplementation3.

indications.text:
Vitamin B2 (riboflavin) is a water-soluble B vitamin that helps maintain the integrity of mucous membranes, skin, eyes and the nervous system.
Riboflavin is mostly present in the body as a component of two coenzymes: Flavin mononucleotide (FMN) and Flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD).
Common clinical symptoms of riboflavin deficiency include inflammation of the throat, mouth (stomatitis), and tongue (glossitis); cracking of the tissue around the corners of the mouth (angular cheilitis) and moist, red, scaly skin.
Vitamin B2 is essential for the activation of other B complex vitamins. FAD is required for the formation of niacin from tryptophan and FMN is required for the formation of the active vitamin B6. Vitamin B2 also participates in folate metabolism. FAD is a cofactor for
methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase (MTHRF), which converts folate into its active form.
Vitamin B2 promotes normal growth and tissue repair. It is required for the growth of skin, hair and nails and a deficiency of vitamin B2 can lengthen wound healing time.
Vitamin B2 helps maintain a healthy immune system. It is required for humoral antibody formation and helps maintain tissue barriers to infection.
Antioxidant
Migraines
Several studies have shown vitamin B2 to be an effective prophylactic to reduce the incidence of migraines.
A preliminary open pilot study of 49 patients with migraine (45 without aura, 4 with aura) found 400mg of riboflavin with or without aspirin for 3 months resulted in a 68.2% improvement in migraine severity. Eighty percent of patients treated with riboflavin alone had a 50% or greater reduction in monthly migraine days1.
Following this, a double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled study investigated the effects of 400mg riboflavin or placebo daily for 3 months on 55 patients with migraine. Riboflavin was found to be superior to placebo in reducing attack frequency (p=0.005) and headache days (p=0.012). For headache days, the number of patient responders (at least 50% improvement) was 15% for placebo and 59% for riboflavin (p=0.002; NNT 2.3)2.
More recently, a double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled study involving 98 patients receiving either 400mg riboflavin daily or placebo for 3 months was performed. The duration and frequency of headache were significantly less in the second and third months of the study in the riboflavin group vs placebo (p=0.012 and p=0.001, respectively)3.
A 2017 systematic review concluded that riboflavin is a well-tolerated and inexpensive treatment, demonstrating efficacy in the reduction of adult patient’s migraine headache frequency as well as duration4.
Vitamin B2 plays an important role in the body’s antioxidant defence
network. FAD is a cofactor for glutathione reductase, which recycles oxidised glutathione.
Vitamin B2, due to its role in antioxidant systems, helps maintain healthy eyes. Glutathione reductase is involved the protection of the lens from free radical damage.
Energy
FMN and FAD are involved in energy metabolism and the release of energy from nutrients in all body cells. FAD is involved in the citric acid cycle, while FMN has a role in the electron transport chain.
Vitamin B2 aids in the metabolism of carbohydrates, fats and proteins, helping to convert food into energy.
Cardiovascular health
Due to its role in folate metabolism, vitamin B2 is important for homocysteine metabolism and, therefore, helps maintain a healthy cardiovascular system.
Vitamin B2 is also important for the formation of haemoglobin which helps transport oxygen in red blood cells and, therefore, helps maintain normal blood.
There is a correlation between plasma levels of vitamin B2 and homocysteine levels, with high homocysteine levels showing low riboflavin status. High homocysteine levels are associated with a higher risk of cardiovascular conditions.

Caution in individuals with gout. Large doses of vitamin B3 can reduce urinary excretion of uric acid (a risk factor for gout).
concentrations in the liver, muscles, kidneys and heart. Excess vitamin
B3 is methylated in the liver and excreted in the urine.
Vitamin B3 can be formed in the body from the amino acid tryptophan, however, it takes approximately 60mg of tryptophan to form 1mg of niacin, with an approximate conversion rate of 60:1. This conversion requires adequate iron, riboflavin and vitamin B6.
As tryptophan is also a precursor to serotonin and dietary tryptophan is preferentially converted to vitamin B3 in deficiency states, low levels of vitamin B3 can result in serotonin depletion and mood alterations.
Energy
Vitamin B3 is used in the body in two coenzyme forms – nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD) and nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate (NADP), which participate in over 200 metabolic reactions.
Vitamin B3, as NAD and NADP, plays a major role in the metabolism of carbohydrate, proteins, fats and alcohol. NAD acts as an electron and hydrogen acceptor in glycolysis and the citric acid cycle. NADP is primarily involved in fatty acid biosynthesis.
Skin health
Vitamin B3, in the form of nicotinamide, supports skin health and DNA repair and has been shown to have a protective effect against damage caused by UV radiation. It prevents the ATP depletion and glycolytic blockade induced by UV radiation, boosting cellular energy and enhancing DNA repair in the skin.
A double-blind, randomised, placebo controlled crossover trial examined the effects of oral nicotinamide on UV exposure in 61 volunteers. Significant immunosuppression occurred in a UV dose-dependent manner in the presence of placebo. Oral nicotinamide, at doses of either 500mg or 1500mg daily, were well tolerated and significantly reduced UV immunosuppression with no immune effects in unirradiated skin1.
A phase 3, double-blind, randomised, controlled trial using 500mg of nicotinamide twice daily substantiated the benefits of vitamin B3 in supporting skin health and protecting skin from the damaging effects of the sun2.

indications.text:
Vitamin B5, also known as pantothenic acid, is a water-soluble B complex vitamin that is widely distributed throughout the food chain.
Pantothenic acid gets its name from the Greek ‘panto’, which means ‘everywhere’ and refers to the ubiquitous nature of this nutrient.
Vitamin B5 is a component of coenzyme A (CoA), the biologically active form of pantothenic acid, which is involved in over 100 metabolic reactions in the body. It is essential for the breakdown of carbohydrates, proteins, lipids and alcohol, the formation of fatty acids, cholesterol, bile acids and steroid hormones, and is involved in energy metabolism.
Major dietary sources of vitamin B5 include chicken, beef, potatoes, oats, tomato products, liver, kidney, egg yolks and whole grains. Vitamin B5 is easily destroyed by food processing, including freezing, canning and refining processes.
Approximately 50% of dietary vitamin B5 is absorbed1. It is absorbed in the jejunum and excreted in the urine. There is currently no upper limit for this vitamin as no toxic effects have been reported.
Pantothenic acid is the most common supplemental form of vitamin B5. It is comprises 91.5% pantothenic acid and 7.5% calcium.
Nervous system
Vitamin B5 supports nervous system health.
CoA is a cofactor in the synthesis of the neurotransmitter acetylcholine, which is involved in learning, memory and mood.
Vitamin B5 is often referred to as the ‘anti-stress’ vitamin, as it is necessary for adrenal function and a healthy stress response. It is involved in the production of glucocorticoids and other adrenal
hormones, including cortisol. Vitamin B5 has been found to enhance adrenal cortical function in animals and may lower secretion of cortisol in periods of stress.
Skin health
Vitamin B5 helps regulate epidermal barrier function and keratinocyte differentiation via CoA metabolism and plays an essential role in normal epithelial function.
Acne is a common skin condition that affects the hair follicles associated with an oil gland. It can present with inflammatory or non-inflammatory lesions.
A randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled study looked at the effects of high-strength pantothenic acid in adults previously
diagnosed with mild to moderate acne vulgaris. Forty-eight subjects were randomised to pantothenic acid (2.2g) or placebo for 12 weeks. There was a significant mean reduction in total lesion count in the pantothenic acid group versus placebo at week 12 (p=0.0197)2.
Another open-label, single arm study in 10 healthy adults diagnosed with mild to moderate acne found that pantothenic acid reduced the number of facial skin blemishes by 56% after 8 weeks3.

indications.text:
Vitex agnus-castus (Chaste tree) has a long history of traditional use in Western herbal medicine (WHM) for the relief of menstrual irregularities and symptoms of premenstrual tension (PMT).
The dried fruit from the Vitex plant contains several active constituents including flavonoids, iridoids, alkaloids and volatile oils.
The mode of action of Vitex is multifaceted. Vitex acts on dopamine (D2) receptors in the anterior pituitary gland, decreasing high prolactin levels. Prolactin is a hormone that primarily functions to help women produce milk after childbirth. However, in non-breastfeeding mothers, elevated prolactin can block the production of other hormones in the body, including oestrogen and progesterone. Elevated prolactin levels are associated with menstrual irregularities and symptoms of PMT1.
Low doses of Vitex have been shown to increase luteinising hormone (LH) while decreasing follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH), working indirectly on achieving oestrogen and progesterone balance within the body. Oestrogen dominance in females is linked to mood disorders, including PMS, and menstrual irregularities.
It is recommended Vitex be taken in the morning, before breakfast, as this is the time the pituitary gland is the most receptive.
Premenstrual syndrome
Premenstrual syndrome (PMS) is a combination of emotional, physical, psychological and mood disturbances that generally occur after a female ovulates and before the onset of a menstrual period.
Emotional symptoms can include irritability, crying, oversensitivity and mood swings, while physical symptoms may present as fatigue, bloating, breast tenderness, skin issues such as acne or appetite changes and food cravings.
It is estimated that as many as 90% of women experience at least one PMS symptom most months and about 50% of women experience several PMS symptoms each month2.
For some women who suffer from PMS, the symptoms are severe enough to interfere with regular day-to-day activities.
Vitex 1000 for PMS
Several clinical studies have been conducted on Vitex for premenstrual syndrome. A phytopharmaceutical formulation of an extract of Vitex fruit was used in 1634 females suffering from PMS symptoms. Self-assessment questionnaires were used to assess symptoms such as headache, anger, irritability, mood, breast fullness and bloating. After taking Vitex for three menstrual cycles, 93% of females reported either a decrease in the number of symptoms or complete cessation of complaints3.
A further study of 178 women with symptoms of PMS tested against placebo demonstrated a statistically significant improvement against symptoms of irritability, mood alteration, anger, headache, breast fullness and bloating4.
Trickey, R. (2011). Women, Hormones & the Menstrual Cycle (2nd ed). Allen & Unwin.
Vitex 1000 for menstrual regulation
Irregular periods can be caused by many factors, including but not limited to, sporadic ovulation, decreased progesterone or increased prolactin.
Vitex works by increasing the release of luteinizing hormone from the pituitary gland, which raises progesterone and normalises the second half of the menstrual cycle.
Vitex & the oral contraceptive pill (OCP)
Vitex is generally not considered suitable to be used alongside the OCP.
Vitex may reduce the effectiveness of contraceptives as it can act as a precursor to the hormones involved in ovulation. This may negate the ovulation-inhibiting effects of the OCP. As a result, women using Vitex alongside birth control could experience an increased risk of unplanned pregnancy5.
High strength	✓ PMS relief	✓ Menstrual cycle regulation	✓ One-a-day dose

cautions.text:
Avoid use in individuals with tumours sensitive to oestrogen or progesterone.
Vitex is not generally recommended in females under 20 years of age as the natural hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis can be easily disrupted.
Vitex is most effective during the first three to six months of use. After that, its effect on the pituitary starts to diminish. It is recommended to take a break from Vitex for two months before resuming use.
Not recommended during pregnancy without medical advice and breastfeeding due to insufficient studies relating to safety.

interactions.interaction_text:
Contraindicated with fertility drugs or IVF – the addition of Vitex could potentially cause hyperstimulation of the ovaries.
Caution with hormone replacement therapy, oral contraceptive pills and progesterone drugs – given Vitex’s hormone modulating effect, it may theoretically interfere with the action of these drugs.
